$$

If $Y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$

To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that since the values of $X$ are $0<x<1,$ $Y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0<x<1,$ we have $y>0.$

![](images/5a/5a2a6f4c5e26819af509e9347fb7aff230927bdd9192ad10a48ce9c951c7be80.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $y>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(-\operatorname{ln}⁡X\le y) \\  & =P(\operatorname{ln}⁡X\ge -y) \\  & =P(X\ge {e}^{-y}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}({e}^{-y})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $y>0,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-{e}^{-y})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}({e}^{-y}) \\  & ={e}^{-y}\cdot {f}_{X}({e}^{-y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={e}^{-y}\cdot {f}_{X}({e}^{-y}) \\  & ={e}^{-y}\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y}\, & y>0 \\ 0\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3})+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3},{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3},{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3})+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{3}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$, the given set is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is false since the vector ${b}_{3}$ can't be written as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}.$ But then

$$

Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\{{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}{b}_{3}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent. Hence, the given set is not a basis for $V.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}({b}_{1}+{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}({b}_{1}+{b}_{3})
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

The critical points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(a)$ does not exist, where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}8{x}^{3}+16x{y}^{2}-16x & \,16{x}^{2}y+12y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}8{x}^{3}+16x{y}^{2}-16x=0 \\ 16{x}^{2}y+12y=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}8x({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2)=0 \\ 4y(4{x}^{2}+3)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since $4{x}^{2}+3\ne 0,$ from the second equation of the system, we obtain that

$$
y=0.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}8x({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ 8x({x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ 8x({x}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ x & =0,\pm \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm \sqrt{2},0)$ and $(0,0).$

Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these points, they are also stationary points.

Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|2x/3|}}{3},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}h(x),\, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2},\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the function $h(x).$

Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{2x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{2x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x)$, the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(x)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\text{ }\text{d}x,
$$

where $f(x)$ is the probability density function of $X.$ 

In this problem, the break point $X$ is chosen uniformly from $[0,2]$, so the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2},\,\,\,\,\,\,0\le x<2.
$$

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $2-X.$ The longer of the two pieces, $Y$, is therefore given by

$$
Y=\text{max}(X,2-X).
$$

Therefore, we define

$$
r(x)=\text{max}(x,2-x).
$$

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

- if $0\le x\le 1$, then $x\le 2-x$, so the longer piece has length $2-x$,

- if $1<x\le 2$, then $x>2-x$, so the longer piece has length $x.$

Therefore,

$$
r(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}2-x, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ x, & 1<x\le 2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[\text{max}(X,2-X)] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-x)\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[2x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{2}(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the expected length of the longer piece is $\frac{3}{2}.$

f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}, & x\ge 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The marginal CDF ${F}_{X}(x)$ of $X$ is given by

$$
{F}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ g(x), & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

What is the function $g(x)?$

If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) &={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $x\ge 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}{[{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $X$ for $x\ge 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}{f}_{X}(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{u}]}_{1}^{x} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${F}_{X}(x)$ is

$$
{F}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ 1-\frac{1}{x}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, $g(x)=1-\frac{1}{x}.$

Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x+y}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2+2y-0) \\  & =\frac{2(y+1)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(y+1)}{3}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0\le x\le 2,0\le y\le 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{x+y}{3}\right)}{\left(\frac{2(y+1)}{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{2(y+1)}.\end{aligned}

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-2x-y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{-y}\lim_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{b}{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{-y}\lim_{b\to \infty }\left(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2}\right){|}_{0}^{b} \\  & ={e}^{-y}\lim_{b\to \infty }(1-{e}^{-2b}) \\  & ={e}^{-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

In general, if $X$ follows a discrete uniform distribution over a set $S,$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{|S|}, & x\in S \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, we have $X∼U\{1,2,…,5\},$ and the set $S=\{1,2,…,5\}$ has $|S|=5-1+1=5$ items. So, we have

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}, & x=1,2,…,5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In $S,$ the items that satisfy $X\le 2$ are $1,2.$ There are $2$ of these elements. Therefore,

$$
P(X\le 2)=2\cdot \frac{1}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(x+2y)}{2}, & \,0\le y\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

Find $P(X<\frac{2}{5}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{5}).$

Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{y}^{1}\frac{3(x+2y)}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{y}^{1}(x+2y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2xy]}_{x=y}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+2y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\frac{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0\le y\le x\le 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{3(x+2y)}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}, & \,0\le y\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

Find $P(X\le 2,Y\le 3).$

Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,3]\times [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y, & \,0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2} \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2,Y\le 3) & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2}{9}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}x[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(2)^{2}}{9}-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $144?$ 

$$
\text{I.}\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}\right.\,\text{II.}\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x≡8 & (\text{mod}\,16)\end{aligned}\right.\,\text{III.}\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,24)\end{aligned}\right.\,
$$

The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem does *not* apply to system I since $3$ and $6$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(3,6)=3>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system II. The numbers $9$ and $16$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $9\cdot 16=144.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system III since $6$ and $24$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,24)=6>1
$$

So, the correct answer is "II only."

$A$ is invertible $$

$$  

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}), & -1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the expected value of $Y.$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $-1\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{3}{8}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{8}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=-1}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{8}[\frac{1}{3}\cdot {1}^{3}+1\cdot {y}^{2}-(-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})] \\  & =\frac{3}{8}(\frac{2}{3}+2{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4}, & -1\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}y\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{y}{4}+\frac{3{y}^{3}}{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3{y}^{4}}{16}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{3}{16})-(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{3}{16}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}, & x\ge 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the expected value of $X.$

The marginal density function for $X$ for $x\ge 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{6{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}{[{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}, & x\ge 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\cdot {f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\lim_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\lim_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2\lim_{b\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{b}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$

$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<2 \\ h(x),\, & 2\le x\le 5 \\ 1,\, & x>5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the function $h(x).$

Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $2\le x\le 5,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<2 \\ {\int }_{2}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 2\le x\le 5 \\ 1, & x>5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{x}\frac{2}{9}(5-t)\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={(\frac{10}{9}t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{9})|}_{2}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{10x}{9}-\frac{16}{9} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}({x}^{2}-10x+16) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(x-8)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$

Find the joint PDF $f(x,y)$ for $0\le x\le 1,\,y\ge 1.$

Since the partial derivatives of $F(x,y)$ are defined, the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y).
$$

For $0\le x\le 1$ and $y\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}(y-1)}{y}\right)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{y})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent continuous random variables with marginal CDFs ${F}_{X}(x)$ and ${F}_{Y}(y),$ respectively, then the corresponding joint CDF of $F(x,y)$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)={F}_{X}(x)\cdot {F}_{Y}(y).
$$

Therefore, for $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge 1,$ the joint CDF for our random variables is 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & ={F}_{X}(x)\cdot {F}_{Y}(y) \\  & =(1-{e}^{1-x})(1-\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}-{e}^{1-x}+\frac{{e}^{1-x}}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the joint CDF is

$$
F(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}-{e}^{1-x}+\frac{{e}^{1-x}}{{y}^{3}}, & x\ge 1,\,y\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $$
\displaystyle \,⇔\,\left\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{Col}(A)⊂{R}^{n},$ then  $\text{nullity}(A)=0.$* $\,\times$

By the invertible matrix theorem, if  $\text{Col}(A)$ is not ${R}^{n}$ then  $A$ is not an invertible matrix and  so we must have $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{Col}(A)⊂{R}^{n},$ then  $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}.$* $\,✓$

Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem, if  $\text{Col}(A)$ is not ${R}^{n}$ then  $A$ is not an invertible matrix and  so we must have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{Col}(A)⊂{R}^{n},$ then  $det(A)=0.$* $\,✓$  

Since $\text{Col}(A)⊂{R}^{n},$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, $A$ is not invertible, which means $det(A)=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$A$ is invertible $$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix,  then  $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}.$* $\,\times$ 

Since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem,  we have $\text{Null}(A)=\{0\}.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix,  then $\text{rank}(A)=3.$* $\,✓$

*If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix,  then $Ax=0$ has only the trivial solution.* $\,✓$

If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) &={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $x\ge 0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(x+y)}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[-{e}^{-(x+y)}]}_{y=0}^{y=\infty } \\  & =0+{e}^{-(x+0)} \\  & ={e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}, & x\ge 0, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1\le X<10) & ={\int }_{-1}^{10}{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{10}{e}^{-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={[-{e}^{-x}]}_{0}^{10} \\  & =-{e}^{-10}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{10}}.\end{aligned}

$$

Find the expected value of $X.$

The marginal density function for $X$ for $0\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}, & 0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\cdot {f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-0) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$

Find $P(X<Y<\frac{3}{2}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{6}).$

Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$  

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}, & \,-1\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $-1\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})}{(\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}, & \,-1\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<Y<\frac{3}{2}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{6}) & =P(\frac{1}{6}<Y<\frac{3}{2}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ={\int }_{1/6}^{3/2}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{1}{6})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1/6}^{3/2}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{9}]}_{1/6}^{3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\frac{27}{8}-\frac{1}{216}) \\  & =\frac{91}{243}.\end{aligned}
$$

f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[165,290],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{125}, & 165\le x\le 290 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 250) & ={\int }_{165}^{250}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{165}^{250}\frac{1}{125}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{125}|}_{165}^{250} \\  & =\frac{250}{125}-\frac{165}{125} \\  & =\frac{17}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ in the first equation is $1,$ while in the second equation it is $5.$

If we multiply the first equation by $-5,$ then the $x$-coefficient will become $-5,$ which will cancel with the coefficient of $5$ in the second equation.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(\,x+3y=7\,)\,\times (-5) \\ 5x+4y=2\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-5x-15y &=-35 \\ 5x+4y &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $x$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{rl}-\cancel{5x}-15y & =-35 \\ \cancel{5x}+4y & =2 \\ \hline (-15y+4y) & =(-35+2) \\ -11y & =-33 \\ y & =3\end{array}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=3.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=3$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+3y & =7 \\ x+3(3) & =7 \\ x+9 & =7 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2,\,y=3,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,3).$

Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}},\, & 1<x<8 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $Y=\sqrt[3]{X},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$

To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=\sqrt[3]{X}$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $1<x<8,$ we have $1<y<2.$

![](images/21/21d19426e86916c123e898bf5427ef858784a601eedb861ba55e22855912005c.png)

*Note: Image not drawn to scale.*

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1<y<2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\sqrt[3]{X}\le y) \\  & =P(X\le {y}^{3}) \\  & =F({y}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $1<y<2,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}({y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}({y}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =3{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}({y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{({y}^{3})^{2}}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}1,\, & 1<y<2 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function ${f}_{X}$ and $Y=u(X),$ where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)|, & y\text{ is between }u(a)\text{ and }u(b) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, we have $Y=(1-X)^{3}.$ The transformation $u(x)=(1-x)^{3}$ is strictly monotonically *decreasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find ${u}^{-1}(y)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u(y) & =(1-y)^{3} \\ y & =(1-{u}^{-1}(y))^{3} \\ {u}^{-1}(y) & =1-\sqrt[3]{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $({u}^{-1})^{′}(y):$

$$
({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)=-\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero ${f}_{Y},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)| \\  & ={f}_{X}(1-\sqrt[3]{y})\cdot |-\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}| \\  & =3(1-[1-\sqrt[3]{y}])^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}} \\  & =3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u(0)=1,\,u(1)=0.
$$

$$

{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)|, & y\text{ is between }u(a)\text{ and }u(b) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, we have $Y=\frac{1}{3}X+1.$ The transformation $u(x)=\frac{1}{3}x+1$ is strictly monotonically *increasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find ${u}^{-1}(y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u(y) & =\frac{1}{3}y+1\text{ } \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{-1}(y)+1 \\ {u}^{-1}(y) & =3y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $({u}^{-1})^{′}(y):$

$$
({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)=3
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero ${f}_{Y},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)| \\  & ={f}_{X}(3y-3)\cdot |3| \\  & =3(3y-3)^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =81(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${f}_{X}$ is nonzero on $0<x<1,$ the bounds are $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we have

$$
u(0)=1,\,u(1)=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the probability distribution of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}81(y-1)^{2}, & 1<y<\frac{4}{3} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

Here, we have $Y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡X.$ The transformation $u(x)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is strictly monotonically *decreasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find ${u}^{-1}(y)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u(y) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ y & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({u}^{-1}(y)) \\ {u}^{-1}(y) & ={e}^{-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $({u}^{-1})^{′}(y):$

$$
({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)=-{e}^{-y}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero ${f}_{Y},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)| \\  & ={f}_{X}({e}^{-y})\cdot |-{e}^{-y}| \\  & =\frac{1}{({e}^{-y})^{2}}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2y}}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\  & ={e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${f}_{X}$ is nonzero on $x\ge 1,$ the bounds are $a=1$ and $b\to \infty ,$ we have

$$

$$
F(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1\,\text{or}\,y<-1 \\ \frac{({x}^{2}-1)({y}^{3}+1)}{2{x}^{2}}, & x\ge 1,\,-1\le y\le 1 \\ {F}_{X}(x), & x\ge 1,\,y>1.\end{aligned}\right.

Find the joint PDF $f(x,y)$ for $x\ge 1,\,-1\le y\le 1.$

Since the partial derivatives of $F(x,y)$ are defined, the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y).
$$

For $x\ge 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{({x}^{2}-1)({y}^{3}+1)}{2{x}^{2}}\right)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{2{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+1)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{2{x}^{2}}\cdot 3{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Otherwise, $f(x,y)=0.$
